title: PLC Memory Addressing: I, Q, M and Friends
oneLiner: PLC memory isn't a flat address space the way a general computer's RAM is -- it's organized into named REGIONS by what kind of thing each bit represents.
keyTakeaway: I, Q, and M addresses look similar but mean fundamentally different things: I and Q are wired to the physical world (inputs and outputs respectively) and get overwritten by the scan cycle's Read Inputs/Write Outputs phases, while M is pure internal state the program controls entirely itself -- confusing an M bit for a Q bit (or vice versa) is a real, easy-to-make mistake with real consequences.
explanation:
A general-purpose computer's RAM (see Computer Architecture) is a flat address space -- any byte can hold anything, and it's up to the program to remember what's stored where. Classic PLC memory is organized differently: addresses are grouped into named regions by what kind of thing they represent, traditionally prefixed by a letter -- I for Input, Q for Output (some platforms use O), M for internal Memory/markers, plus dedicated regions for Timers (T) and Counters (C). In Siemens and IEC style an address like I1.3 (IEC writes %IX1.3) means "input byte 1, bit 3" -- the exact physical wire a sensor is connected to; outputs and markers follow the same pattern (Q0.0, M3.2). Allen-Bradley's older SLC and PLC-5 controllers write the same idea differently: I:1/3 is "input module in slot 1, bit 3", outputs are O:2/0, internal bits are B3:0/5 and a timer's done bit is T4:0/DN. The two styles don't mix, so "Q:1/0" or "M:3/2" is valid in neither.

The critical distinction is what CONTROLS each region. I addresses are overwritten by the scan cycle's Read Inputs phase every single scan -- the program can read an I bit but never usefully write to it, since the next scan just overwrites it from the physical input again. Q addresses are written by the program during Execute Program and pushed to the physical outputs during Write Outputs -- the program controls them, the physical world just receives them. M addresses are neither: they're not wired to anything physical at all, purely internal scratch state the program uses to remember something between rungs, or between scans (a "seal-in" bit keeping a motor running after its start button releases, a step counter in a sequence) -- this is the region newcomers most often reach for once they need "memory" that isn't tied to a real wire.

Modern PLC platforms (Studio 5000, TIA Portal) mostly replace this letter-prefix addressing with named TAGS (StartButton, ConveyorRunning, instead of I:1/0 or Q0.0, M3.2) -- readable names instead of cryptic coordinates -- but the underlying regions (physical input, physical output, internal memory) are exactly the same concept underneath, just with better names on top. Reading legacy code (and a lot of running industrial equipment still is legacy code) still means recognizing I/Q/M (or I/O/B) at a glance.
